intro: This Year 9 Maths handout introduces changing the subject of a formula through inverse operations, fractions and brackets. It is designed for KS3 classroom teaching, supported independent practice and revision, without tying the material to a GCSE exam board.

Each of the four teaching sections contains a core concept, one worked example and four class exercises, with space to show working. The final two pages provide worked solutions for all 16 exercises, marking points and a note that equivalent rearrangements are accepted.
covers: Identifying the subject and applying inverse operations to both sides
Removing fractions and checking non-zero divisors
Rearranging brackets using efficient choices
Checking rearrangements by substitution
Applications involving perimeter, temperature and taxi fares
page.scope_note: Part 01 of a two-part Year 9 sequence. Work through Foundations before Next Steps if fractions, brackets or inverse operations are not yet secure. The included marking points are classroom guidance, not an official examination mark scheme.

key_ideas.heading: Apply the same operation to both sides
key_ideas.text: The subject is the letter on its own. For v = u + at, subtract u and divide by t to obtain a = (v - u)/t, with t ≠ 0.

key_ideas.heading: Keep the whole numerator together
key_ideas.text: For y = (x - 5)/3, multiplying by 3 gives 3y = x - 5, then x = 3y + 5. A fraction bar groups its entire numerator.

key_ideas.heading: Choose an efficient route and check it
key_ideas.text: For P = 2(l + w), divide by 2 before subtracting l: w = P/2 - l. Check by substituting allowed values into the original formula.

page.subtitle: Free six-page KS3 classroom handout extending rearrangement skills, with stretch questions and worked solutions.
intro: This handout is for Year 9 students ready to move beyond basic inverse operations, fractions and brackets. It extends changing-the-subject work to square roots, factorising and target-letter terms on both sides, with extension questions for additional challenge.

The four sections each contain a core concept, worked example and four class exercises, giving 16 exercises in total. The final two pages supply worked solutions and marking points. Foundations is the recommended starting point if the prerequisite skills need practice.
covers: Isolating squares before taking square roots
Choosing positive roots for non-negative lengths and using ± roots in algebra
Collecting and factorising target-letter terms
Handling a target letter on both sides
Non-zero denominators, restrictions and extension reasoning
Applying rearrangement to circle area, rectangle perimeter and equal costs
page.scope_note: Part 02 of a two-part Year 9 sequence, including stretch questions. Students should be comfortable with the Foundations techniques. This is a KS3 classroom resource, not an exam-board-specific GCSE worksheet; marking points are classroom guidance.

key_ideas.heading: Isolate the square and choose the appropriate root
key_ideas.text: For A = πr² with r ≥ 0, r = √(A/π). For unrestricted real x with y = x², use x = ±√y when y ≥ 0; the two roots coincide when y = 0.

key_ideas.heading: Factorise to isolate repeated target letters
key_ideas.text: For p = ax + bx + d, collect the x terms: p - d = x(a + b). Then x = (p - d)/(a + b), provided a + b ≠ 0.

key_ideas.heading: Check restrictions before dividing
key_ideas.text: For ax + b = cx + d, x = (d - b)/(a - c) only when a ≠ c. If the target terms cancel, inspect the remaining equality rather than dividing by zero.

page.subtitle: Free 11-page PDF on reference angles, CAST, double angles and domains for Edexcel International A-Level Pure Mathematics 3.

alignment.framework: Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level Mathematics

intro: These free revision notes help Edexcel International A-Level P3 students find every solution of a trigonometric equation within its stated domain, rather than relying only on the calculator's principal value.

The 11-page handout follows a consistent sequence: reference angle, CAST quadrants, one-cycle solutions, then extend to the required interval. It includes a CAST diagram, worked examples, quick checks, nine exam-style targeted practice questions, answers and a final exam checklist.
covers: Reference angles, principal values and the CAST sign pattern
Solving sine, cosine and tangent equations in radians and degrees
Intervals wider than one cycle and tangent periodicity
Transforming the domain for multiple and shifted angles
Double-angle identities, reciprocal functions and quadratic trig equations
Connecting harmonic form to angle-solving, plus practice and answers
page.scope_note: This is focused P3 trigonometry revision, not a complete P3 revision pack. Answers are supplied for the practice exercises, including all nine exam-style questions; these are not full worked solutions for every question. The harmonic-form section explains the method without specifying a numerical solution domain.

key_ideas.heading: Use CAST after finding the reference angle
key_ideas.text: Find a positive acute reference angle for non-axis cases, then use the original sign to select quadrants: all functions are positive in I, sine in II, tangent in III and cosine in IV. Handle axis cases separately.

key_ideas.heading: Extend solutions to the whole domain
key_ideas.text: Sine and cosine repeat every 2π radians or 360°. Tangent repeats every π radians or 180°. Add or subtract the relevant period and retain only values in the stated interval, respecting open and closed endpoints.

key_ideas.heading: Transform the inside-angle interval first
key_ideas.text: For sin 2x = 3/4 with 0 < x < π, first solve in 0 < 2x < 2π, then divide by two. For a shifted expression such as 2x - 70°, transform both endpoints before applying CAST and return to x at the end.

key_ideas.heading: Simplify with identities and solve every branch
key_ideas.text: Use sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x and cos 2x = 2 cos²x - 1 = 1 - 2 sin²x to simplify equations. When factorising gives several possible sine or cosine values, solve every valid branch and check the original equation and domain.

page.subtitle: Free 8-page PDF revision notes for Edexcel International A-Level Pure Mathematics 3.

alignment.framework: Pearson Edexcel International Advanced Level Mathematics

intro: These free revision notes are for students revising Edexcel International A-Level Pure Mathematics 3 (P3, paper code WMA13). They focus on harmonic equations: combining sine and cosine terms into one trigonometric expression and using that form to answer questions.

The 8-page PDF moves from coefficient matching and angle signs to maximum, minimum and range questions, then solving equations in a shifted interval. It includes worked examples, short Try It exercises, common pitfalls, targeted practice and an answers and quick-check page.
covers: Rewriting a sin x + b cos x as R sin(x + α) or R cos(x - α)
Finding R = √(a² + b²) and comparing coefficients
Checking the signs and quadrants of the angle α
Maximum, minimum and range, including a constant vertical shift
Solving harmonic equations using the shifted-angle interval
Targeted practice, exam-style reasoning and selected answers
page.scope_note: This is one P3 topic area, not a complete P3 revision pack. Answers are provided for Sections 1, 2, 3, 5 and 7; the Section 4 Try It exercises are left for self-checking by expansion.

key_ideas.heading: Find R, then compare coefficients
key_ideas.text: For R sin(x + α), expansion gives R cos α = a and R sin α = b. With non-zero coefficients, R = √(a² + b²). For R cos(x - α), the coefficient equations change to R sin α = a and R cos α = b. Always expand the form requested in the question.

key_ideas.heading: Check angle signs before using your calculator
key_ideas.text: The signs of the original coefficients determine the signs of sin α and cos α. For example, 3 sin x - 4 cos x = 5 sin(x - α), with α = tan⁻¹(4/3). Expand your final expression to check that both coefficient signs match.

key_ideas.heading: Read maximum, minimum and range from harmonic form
key_ideas.text: For unrestricted real x, a sin x + b cos x + c has maximum c + R, minimum c - R and range [c - R, c + R]. The handout example y = 6 + 3 sin x - 4 cos x therefore has range [1, 11]. On a restricted interval, check whether the extrema occur within that interval.

key_ideas.heading: Solve in the shifted interval, then return to x
key_ideas.text: For 3 sin x + 4 cos x = 2 with 0 ≤ x < 2π, put α = tan⁻¹(4/3) and θ = x + α. Solve sin θ = 0.4 in α ≤ θ < 2π + α. With β = sin⁻¹(0.4), use θ = π - β or 2π + β, then subtract α. The solutions are x ≈ 1.8028 and 5.7674 radians.

intro: These free revision notes are for students taking Edexcel International A-Level Pure Mathematics 3 (P3, paper code WMA13). They focus on one topic area: functions, composite functions, inverse functions, and domain and range.
They are written for students who want a structured summary of this topic while revising for P3, and for anyone studying functions at A-Level who wants to strengthen the foundations.
covers: Functions and function notation
Composite functions
Inverse functions
Domain and range
page.scope_note: The notes cover this one topic area of P3. They are not a complete P3 revision pack.

key_ideas.heading: Functions and function notation
key_ideas.text: A function assigns exactly one output to each input in its domain. f(x) is the output when the function f is applied to the input x.

key_ideas.heading: Composite functions
key_ideas.text: The composite function fg(x) means f(g(x)): apply g first, then apply f to the result. The order matters, and in general fg(x) is not the same as gf(x).

key_ideas.heading: Inverse functions
key_ideas.text: The inverse function f⁻¹ reverses the effect of f. It exists only when f is one-to-one. The domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f, the range of f⁻¹ is the domain of f, and the graph of y = f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of y = f(x) in the line y = x.

key_ideas.heading: Domain and range
key_ideas.text: The domain is the set of inputs a function is defined for. The range is the set of outputs it produces from that domain.
